paragraphs: Reconstructing viewed images from brain activity can produce impressive results, but the internal representations often make it difficult to understand what the decoder has learned. This paper adds an interpretable intermediate representation to BrainDiffuser: 214 binary concepts, each answering a concrete question about an image, such as whether it contains a person or depicts an outdoor scene.

A ridge regression first maps fMRI voxel activity into these concept answers. Because this step is linear, its weights can be displayed as spatial maps showing which voxels influence each concept. A second regression converts the concept representation into the CLIP embeddings used to condition image reconstruction. The concepts therefore connect the brain measurements to the generated image through an inspectable stage.

The resulting maps align closely with established visual cortical regions associated with faces, bodies, places, and words. They also suggest that the distribution of activation carries semantic information beyond its location. Reconstruction performance decreases slightly: CLIP similarity falls by no more than 4% across four subjects. The reported tradeoff is substantially greater interpretability with a modest measured performance cost.
neurips-2025-bridging-brains-and-concept.tldr: An interpretable concept layer connects fMRI activity to reconstructed images, revealing semantic brain maps with only a small reported reduction in decoding performance.

paragraphs: Car recognition presents a moving target: models appear, change appearance, and disappear over time. CaMiT makes this temporal evolution available for studying fine-grained vision. It contains 787,000 labeled examples covering 190 car models from 2007–2023, alongside 5.1 million unlabeled examples from 2005–2023. The two portions support learning both with and without explicit labels.

The authors find that static pretraining on car data can compete with large general-purpose models while using resources more efficiently. However, recognition accuracy deteriorates when a model trained for one year's data is evaluated on earlier or later years. They therefore examine continual classification in which the available classes themselves emerge, evolve, or disappear.

Two updating strategies produce positive results: progressively updating the backbone representation and progressively updating the final classifier. The paper also uses temporal metadata consistently during image-generation training, reporting more realistic images than standard generation. Together, these studies make CaMiT useful for investigating how both recognition and generation can adapt to changing object appearance, rather than treating a dataset's visual categories as fixed.
neurips-2025-camit-a-time-aware-car-mode.tldr: CaMiT tracks car models through time and shows benefits from updating recognition models and incorporating temporal information into image generation.

paragraphs: Causal discovery usually seeks relationships among individual variables, but a large collection of such relationships can be difficult to learn and interpret. Researchers may instead care about connections among groups of variables. This paper develops a framework for discovering those group-level relationships in Markov causal systems, with the clusters specified by the user.

The central contribution is a graphical model that encodes knowledge about relationships between clusters while faithfully representing their dependencies and independencies for a given distribution. This matters because grouping variables must preserve the statistical relationships relevant to the desired analysis. The authors also characterize an equivalence class of graphs that express the same cluster-level independence information.

That equivalence class distinguishes relationships the available information can resolve from alternative structures it cannot distinguish. Building on this characterization, the paper supplies a sound and complete discovery algorithm for representing learnable causal relationships between clusters. The contribution is a theoretical basis for causal analysis at a coarser level, potentially improving scalability while presenting relationships at the level researchers actually want to examine.
neurips-2025-causal-discovery-over-clust.tldr: The paper develops graphical models and a sound, complete algorithm for discovering learnable causal relationships among user-defined variable clusters.

paragraphs: Transfer learning uses information from a source problem to help learn a target problem. In high-dimensional models, many existing methods organize this transfer into two regularized steps. Their success depends heavily on the pretrained source model already resembling the target. When the source parameters differ substantially, subsequent fine-tuning can fail to extract useful information.

This paper proposes co-regularization for high-dimensional generalized linear models. Its target-learning process constrains source parameters to remain close to the target parameter. The direction of that constraint is central: it allows the method to exploit beneficial source knowledge without making a strongly mismatched pretrained parameter the foundation of successful fine-tuning.

The theoretical analysis shows that the proposed method accommodates a broader range of sources than the existing two-step frameworks. This supports greater robustness when source and target are less similar, within the setting studied. Extensive empirical studies also support the method's effectiveness. The contribution is therefore both a different way to structure transfer and an analysis explaining why that structure can tolerate more source mismatch.
neurips-2025-co-regularization-enhances-.tldr: Co-regularization enables high-dimensional generalized linear models to benefit from a broader range of source models than existing two-step transfer methods.

paragraphs: In decentralized federated learning, participants train locally and exchange models directly, without a central server coordinating aggregation. This paper examines a form of strategic misconduct within that collaboration. A group of selfish participants seeks a competitive advantage: its final local models should be more accurate than those held by the remaining participants.

The proposed SelfishAttack family pursues that objective by sending carefully constructed local models to non-selfish participants during training rounds. The authors formulate the choice of those models as an optimization problem and develop solutions for different aggregation rules. Their theoretical result establishes that the methods obtain optimal solutions to the formulated optimization problem.

Experiments show that SelfishAttack increases the final accuracy gap between selfish and non-selfish participants. It also produces larger gaps than poisoning attacks adapted to pursue competitive advantage. These findings identify a distinct failure mode for collaborative learning: participants can manipulate what they share to improve their relative position. The relevant outcome is unequal final model quality across collaborators, which makes relative advantage an important attack objective to examine.
neurips-2025-competitive-advantage-attac.tldr: SelfishAttack manipulates exchanged models so that selfish participants gain a larger accuracy advantage in decentralized federated learning.

paragraphs: Brain-computer interfaces need to decode neural activity reliably across recording days. Their performance can drift because the recorded signals change, partly through neuron loss and electrode movement. These changes affect individual recording channels. Earlier approaches align recordings within a shared low-dimensional representation, but substantial signal drift can make that alignment difficult.

CRRL addresses variability directly at the channel level by learning representations intended to remain stable across days. Its channel-rearrangement module handles changes associated with electrode shifts. A separate channel-reconstruction module addresses missing neurons. Together, the modules target two concrete sources of recording instability rather than relying solely on alignment of the overall neural representation.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark brain-computer-interface datasets for cross-day decoding tasks spanning two months. They also report good generalization and compatibility with different neural networks. These results support channel-level invariance as a useful design principle for more stable decoding. Its practical significance is that the representation addresses changes in the recording interface that would otherwise make the same decoding task harder on later days.
neurips-2025-crrl-learning-channel-invar.tldr: CRRL learns stable channel-level neural representations to improve brain-computer-interface decoding across days despite electrode shifts and missing neurons.

paragraphs: Allocating resources requires judgments about fairness as well as economic efficiency. This paper evaluates whether language models make distribution decisions consistent with human preferences and established fairness concepts. The benchmark examines equitability, envy-freeness, and Rawlsian maximin, bringing several distinct views of a desirable allocation into the evaluation.

Across the evaluated models, the authors find a mismatch between generated responses and human distributional preferences. They also find that the models do not successfully use money as a transferable resource to reduce inequality. A further comparison reveals a marked difference for some models when they choose from a predefined menu instead of generating an allocation themselves.

The study also tests sensitivity to changes in meaning, such as intentions or personas, and changes in presentation, such as templates or option order. This broadens the evaluation from the allocation alone to the conditions under which it is elicited. The findings indicate that fairness alignment depends partly on how the decision task is posed, while the paper identifies potential strategies for improving alignment with established fairness principles.
neurips-2025-distributive-fairness-in-la.tldr: Evaluated language models diverge from human distributional preferences, with some responding markedly differently when selecting allocations instead of generating them.

paragraphs: Fast camera motion makes scene reconstruction difficult because ordinary video leaves gaps between frames and can yield inaccurate camera poses. EF-3DGS supplements casually captured video with event-camera measurements. These measurements record pixel-level intensity changes asynchronously, providing motion and scene information during intervals that conventional frames do not observe.

The method combines events with 3D Gaussian Splatting through three components. An event-generation model connects events and frames to supervise reconstruction between frames. Contrast maximization over warped events extracts motion information, refines camera poses, and supplies gradient-domain constraints. Because events lack color information, photometric bundle adjustment and a Fixed-GS training strategy separate structure optimization from color optimization to maintain consistency across views.

The authors evaluate the system on Tanks and Temples and their newly collected RealEv-DAVIS dataset. In challenging high-speed settings, they report up to 3 dB higher PSNR and 40% lower absolute trajectory error than state-of-the-art methods. These results indicate improvements in both reconstruction quality and camera-motion estimation, supporting the value of using event measurements to fill video's temporal gaps.
neurips-2025-ef-3dgs-event-aided-free-tr.tldr: EF-3DGS combines event-camera measurements with video to improve high-speed 3D reconstruction and camera-pose estimation.

paragraphs: Recognizing emotions in conversations benefits from combining multiple kinds of signals, but some signals may be missing. Existing recovery methods often assume complete multimodal training data. That dependence becomes especially problematic when a client consistently lacks a particular modality, because recovered information can lose the meaning of the available conversation.

FedDISC shares recovery capability through federated learning. Clients train diffusion models for individual modalities; these models are aggregated and distributed to clients missing the corresponding signals. This reduces reliance on any single client's having complete data. Within the recovery process, a dialogue graph captures conversational dependencies, while semantic conditioning aligns recovered information with available signals, including context and speaker identity.

The framework also alternates which components remain frozen during aggregation, coordinating optimization of the recovery modules and the emotion classifier. Experiments on IEMOCAP, CMUMOSI, and CMUMOSEI report better emotion classification than existing approaches across different missing-modality patterns. The findings support combining shared recovery models with conversation-aware constraints: access to a reconstruction model matters, but preserving the conversation's meaning also matters for the final classification.
neurips-2025-federated-dialogue-semantic.tldr: FedDISC shares modality-recovery diffusion models across clients while preserving conversational meaning to improve emotion recognition with missing signals.

paragraphs: Semi-asynchronous federated learning balances different ways of coordinating participants that train without exchanging raw data. Within this setting, the paper examines a tradeoff between aggregating gradients and aggregating models. Gradient aggregation offers faster convergence and higher accuracy in the described comparison, but fluctuates more. Model aggregation is steadier, yet converges more slowly and reaches lower accuracy.

FedQS develops a theoretical analysis of these differences and uses it to address variation among clients. Its divide-and-conquer strategy places clients into four types, then adapts their local training according to data-distribution characteristics and available computing resources. This makes client-specific conditions part of the training strategy instead of applying an identical local procedure throughout the federation.

Experiments span computer vision, natural language processing, and real-world tasks. Among the compared methods, FedQS achieves the highest accuracy and lowest loss while ranking among the fastest to converge. The reported results support its aim of combining stability, accuracy, and efficiency. The contribution connects aggregation behavior to client heterogeneity and offers a unified framework for managing their interaction.
neurips-2025-fedqs-optimizing-gradient-a.tldr: FedQS adapts client training to data and computing differences to improve accuracy, stability, and convergence in semi-asynchronous federated learning.

paragraphs: Federated learning can spend substantial communication resources exchanging model updates. Many methods reduce this burden by discarding some updates, often using gradient magnitude to decide what to retain. This paper investigates a different use of the information already available to the server: reusing previous updates for selected layers.

The proposed FedLUAR method first measures how strongly aggregated gradients influence parameter values in each layer. It uses this layer-level metric to choose a small set of layers whose earlier updates will be recycled on the server. The decision therefore depends on the updates' influence on model parameters, and the server continues to use previously communicated information for those layers.

The empirical study finds that recycling can substantially reduce communication while maintaining model accuracy. On AG News, FedLUAR reaches nearly the same accuracy as FedAvg while using only 17% of its communication cost. That example illustrates the intended benefit: earlier updates can retain enough value to support continued learning without requiring equally frequent fresh communication for every layer.
neurips-2025-layer-wise-update-aggregati.tldr: FedLUAR reuses earlier updates for selected model layers, reaching nearly FedAvg's AG News accuracy with 17% of its communication cost.

paragraphs: Estimating gene expression from pathology images could reduce reliance on costly RNA sequencing. Common training objectives compare each predicted expression value with its measured absolute value. However, sequencing procedures, cell variability, random noise, and batch effects make those absolute measurements difficult targets to predict accurately across tissue samples.

This paper changes the learning objective to relative expression patterns. Its explicit assumption is that relative gene-expression levels exhibit consistent patterns across independent experiments, even when noise and batch effects alter absolute values. Under that assumption, relationships among expression levels can provide a more stable training signal than exact numerical measurements.

The authors model these relationships through a loss function called STRank, designed to resist noise and batch effects. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets support the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a change in what image-based prediction is trained to preserve: the relative structure of expression. Its rationale depends on the stated consistency assumption, which explains why learning trends can help when absolute measurements vary between experiments.
neurips-2025-learning-relative-gene-expr.tldr: STRank learns relative gene-expression patterns from pathology images, assuming those relationships remain more consistent across experiments than absolute measurements.

paragraphs: Adversarial training exposes a model to attacks during learning to improve its resistance. For language models, training with concrete adversarial prompts can be expensive. Faster continuous perturbations provide an alternative, but they do not always represent the vulnerabilities exposed by discrete prompt attacks. MIXAT combines these two sources of adversarial examples.

The method uses stronger discrete attacks alongside faster continuous attacks during training. Its evaluation introduces At Least One Attack Success Rate, or ALO-ASR, to capture whether any attack in the evaluated collection succeeds. This emphasizes vulnerability across the attack suite instead of allowing strong performance against some attacks to obscure a successful attack elsewhere.

Across the reported evaluations, MIXAT achieves ALO-ASR below 20%, compared with above 50% for prior defenses, while keeping runtime comparable to continuous-relaxation methods. The authors also examine chat templates, quantization, low-rank adapters, and temperature in deployment-oriented training and evaluation. These analyses reveal additional methodological blind spots. The results support combining attack types as a practical robustness improvement with limited added computation, while the reported success rate still reflects remaining vulnerabilities.
neurips-2025-mixat-combining-continuous-.tldr: MIXAT combines discrete and continuous adversarial training to reduce measured attack success while retaining runtime comparable to continuous-only approaches.

paragraphs: Questions requiring several connected facts challenge retrieval-augmented generation because relevant information may be spread across documents. Graph-based retrieval represents document connections, but matching nodes and constructing subgraphs can introduce irrelevant material or break the coherence of the evidence. NeuroPath organizes retrieval around meaningful paths toward the question's goal.

Inspired by navigational planning associated with place cells, the framework has two stages. Dynamic Path Tracking uses an LLM to follow and prune paths through a knowledge graph. Post-retrieval Completion then combines intermediate reasoning with the original question to clarify the retrieval goal and obtain information missing from the developing reasoning path.

On three multi-hop question-answering datasets, NeuroPath reports average recall improvements of 16.3% at two retrieved results and 13.5% at five over advanced graph-based methods. Compared with iterative retrieval methods, it achieves higher accuracy while reducing token consumption by 22.8%. Evaluations also support robustness across four smaller language models and scalability across task complexities. These findings suggest that tracking and completing coherent evidence paths can improve retrieval quality while reducing the amount of model processing required.
neurips-2025-neuropath-neurobiology-insp.tldr: NeuroPath follows and completes coherent knowledge-graph paths, improving multi-hop retrieval and answer accuracy while reducing token use in reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems often have relatively few observed interactions to learn from. Contrastive learning creates additional training signals by encouraging a node's representations to agree across modified versions of an interaction graph. The paper identifies a problem with this approach: its objective can unintentionally separate a target node from other nodes along its interaction paths.

The proposed Path Enhanced Contrastive Loss uses sampled paths as training examples. One component compares the target node with nodes within a path, while another compares relationships between paths. These complementary comparisons are designed to keep the target close to relevant path nodes. A dedicated sampling method supplies the paths used by the objective.

The complete PECL model builds on LightGCN and introduces a path-enhanced graph-augmentation approach alongside the new loss. Experiments on three real-world datasets report significant recommendation improvements. The contribution makes interaction paths an explicit part of the self-supervised objective, so that learning across graph variations better preserves the relationships the recommender is intended to exploit.
neurips-2025-path-enhanced-contrastive-l.tldr: PECL uses within-path and between-path contrastive learning to preserve useful interaction relationships and improve recommendation on sparse data.

paragraphs: Earth-observation models need to interpret multispectral imagery while operating within practical computing constraints. Simply increasing model size can conflict with applications such as onboard processing or rapid disaster response. PhySwin combines computational efficiency with physical information about the measurements, addressing both concerns within a foundation model for multispectral data.

Its pretraining objectives use radiometric constraints to guide feature learning. An efficient MixMAE formulation adapted to SwinV2 reduces the computation required for scalable pretraining. A spectral embedding component retains spectral detail without increasing the number of tokens processed by the model. These elements connect the measurement properties of the input to an architecture designed for efficient processing.

Pretrained on more than one million Sentinel-2 tiles, PhySwin reports state-of-the-art results, with improvements of 1.32% in segmentation mIoU and 0.80% in change-detection F1. Compared with ViT-based remote-sensing foundation models, inference latency is reduced by up to 14.4 times and computational complexity by up to 43.6 times. The results support improving task performance and efficiency together through physically informed objectives and careful representation design.
neurips-2025-physwin-an-efficient-and-ph.tldr: PhySwin combines physical constraints and efficient multispectral processing to improve Earth-observation results while substantially reducing reported inference costs.

paragraphs: Many learning problems provide only a partial list of correct answers. A photograph may have some people tagged without revealing everyone present, for example. In such settings, an unobserved label is not necessarily incorrect. This paper studies how to learn predictions that balance precision and recall when training supplies positive examples alone.

The authors introduce a Probably Approximately Correct framework in which each hypothesis maps an input to a set of labels. This accommodates richer outputs than a single predicted class and generalizes classical binary, multiclass, and multilabel formulations. Their analysis shows that familiar tools can behave very differently here: empirical risk minimization provably fails even for simple hypothesis classes.

New algorithms achieve optimal sample complexity in the realizable case, where the hypothesis class can represent the target. In the agnostic case, they provide multiplicative approximation guarantees, while additive regret guarantees are impossible in the studied framework. The results clarify both what positive-only feedback allows and why precision-and-recall learning requires methods and guarantees tailored to incomplete observations.
neurips-2025-probably-approximately-prec.tldr: A new learning framework establishes algorithms and limits for predicting label sets with good precision and recall from positive-only feedback.

paragraphs: Predictive confidence sets aim to contain the true outcome at a desired frequency. A guarantee averaged over possible validation datasets does not directly describe what happens after one particular validation dataset has been collected. This paper revisits split-conformal prediction to establish coverage guarantees that condition on that observed validation sample.

The authors provide new arguments showing that split-conformal methods reach coverage near the desired level with high probability over the validation data. They also examine approximate conditional coverage for groups defined by the input variables. This asks whether the prediction set contains the outcome when attention is restricted to a particular group of interest.

For these conditional questions, the paper shows that fitting quantile regression on held-out validation data achieves minimax-optimal coverage guarantees. This establishes a strong statistical justification for a natural procedure within the settings analyzed. Experiments also highlight remaining work on computationally efficient methods for valid predictive inference. The contribution therefore distinguishes stronger forms of coverage and explains how far a held-out-data approach can go toward achieving them.
neurips-2025-sample-conditional-coverage.tldr: The paper strengthens split-conformal coverage guarantees and establishes minimax-optimal guarantees for conditional coverage using held-out quantile regression.

paragraphs: During language-model generation, stored attention keys and values create a growing retrieval burden. Selecting the most relevant cached entries can reduce that burden. Spotlight Attention targets the hashing used to find those entries, arguing that random linear hashing is poorly suited to the narrow, orthogonally arranged distributions of queries and keys found in language models.

The method learns nonlinear hash functions that reshape the query and key embeddings for more effective coding. A Bradley–Terry ranking loss trains the hashing module to support retrieval, using a lightweight framework reported to run in eight hours on a GPU with 16 GB of memory. Specialized CUDA kernels then exploit bitwise operations to make hash-based retrieval fast.

Experiments report substantially better retrieval precision with hash codes at least five times shorter than traditional linear hashing. On one A100 GPU, retrieval over 512,000 tokens takes under 100 microseconds, and end-to-end throughput reaches up to three times vanilla decoding. These results connect better retrieval representations with optimized execution, showing how both contribute to faster generation.
neurips-2025-spotlight-attention-towards.tldr: Spotlight Attention learns nonlinear hashes for accurate, compact KV-cache retrieval and reports up to threefold higher decoding throughput.

paragraphs: Image generators can produce convincing, varied pictures while still missing subjective preferences such as aesthetic appeal or engagement. SPRO addresses the cost and limited diversity of human annotations with a self-play training loop. A vision-language model helps generate, evaluate, and refine outputs using synthetic reward signals tied to preference objectives.

The framework has three stages. SPRO-Prompt trains a guiding vision-language model to create diverse prompts that score well on objectives including PickScore, LAION-Aesthetics, and EngageNet. SPRO-Image fine-tunes the diffusion model using high-reward images obtained from those prompts. SPRO-Multimodal combines prompt and image optimization into an end-to-end alignment process.

Without human-labeled training data, the authors report an average 30% improvement across the measured preference objectives. Learned prompts also transfer across open- and closed-source diffusion models. Self-play discovers unusual strategies, including visual harmony cues for aesthetics and shadow-based cues for engagement. The findings show that optimizing prompts and generated images together can improve these preference-related signals through a self-generated feedback loop.
neurips-2025-spro-improving-image-genera.tldr: SPRO uses multimodal self-play and synthetic rewards to improve image-generation preference objectives without human-labeled training data.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient methods repeatedly use noisy estimates of an objective's gradient to update a model. This paper studies an additional complication: the objective itself depends on unknown nuisance parameters. Those quantities are not the main learning target, yet their presence can shift the optimum and disturb the path taken during optimization.

The authors establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees, describing behavior over finite optimization runs. They show that the classical stochastic gradient algorithm may still converge under appropriate conditions, including Neyman orthogonality. The result explains how suitable structure in the learning problem can protect optimization from the effects of nuisance quantities.

When Neyman orthogonality does not hold, the paper also considers a variant using approximately orthogonalized gradient updates. Under its analyzed conditions, this variant may attain similar convergence rates. Examples connect the theory to orthogonal statistical learning, double machine learning, and causal inference. The contribution identifies both conditions under which ordinary stochastic gradients remain effective and a possible modification when the original objective lacks the needed orthogonality.
neurips-2025-stochastic-gradients-under-.tldr: Finite-run theory shows when stochastic gradients can converge despite unknown nuisance parameters and how approximate orthogonalization may preserve convergence rates.

paragraphs: A contextual cascading bandit recommends an ordered list of items to a user who scans sequentially and stops at the first attractive item. The learner must improve its recommendations through interaction. This paper asks how the list length affects regret, the accumulated performance gap associated with learning instead of making optimal recommendations.

Earlier results suggested that regret grows as lists become longer. The authors prove that it instead decreases once the list is sufficiently long. They use this insight to design an upper-confidence-bound algorithm built on online mirror descent. Its regret bound contains a length-dependent factor capped at one, with an exponentially decreasing term that eventually outweighs the linear contribution of list length.

A nearly matching lower bound complements the algorithm's upper bound, clarifying the dependence on cascade length from both directions. The bounds use respective parameters below one, so the result is more specific than claiming that every increase in list length helps. Experiments support the theoretical findings and the proposed algorithm's effectiveness. The main advance is resolving how sufficiently long cascades can make the learning problem easier in regret terms.
neurips-2025-true-impact-of-cascade-leng.tldr: The paper proves that contextual cascading-bandit regret decreases for sufficiently long recommendation lists and develops an algorithm with nearly matching theoretical bounds.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems commonly infer preferences by connecting users' past interactions to item topics. This paper argues that users' characteristics and social roles also help explain interests and changes in preference. It introduces two explicit tasks: identifying user roles and modeling logical relationships between those roles and item topics.

TagCF addresses these tasks by combining recommendation models with the world knowledge and reasoning capabilities of language models, including multimodal models. It extracts tag-based logic graphs intended to represent dynamic information about users and their behavior. Integration modules then use this graph information to improve recommendations, connecting the extracted relationships to the recommender's predictions.

Online and offline experiments on industrial and public datasets support TagCF's effectiveness. The results suggest that modeling user roles may be a better choice than modeling item topics in the examined settings, rather than establishing a universal ranking between them. The authors also provide empirical evidence that the extracted logic graphs transfer across recommendation tasks. The contribution expands the information a recommender explicitly represents to include relationships between identity, role, and interest.
neurips-2025-who-you-are-matters-bridgin.tldr: TagCF uses language models to connect user roles and item topics through logic graphs, improving recommendations in online and offline experiments.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by drafting and verifying multiple tokens in parallel. Its execution can be inefficient when dynamically chosen speculation patterns meet a runtime designed around static computation. Yggdrasil addresses that mismatch by designing the drafting procedure and execution system together, with latency as the guiding objective.

The system uses context-aware tree drafting to organize candidate continuations. An equal-growth tree structure makes that organization compatible with static execution graphs. Draft selection explicitly accounts for latency, while stage-based scheduling reduces execution overhead. These components connect decisions about what to speculate with the practical cost of running and verifying those decisions.

Yggdrasil supports language models without modifying them and reports speedups of up to 3.98 times over state-of-the-art baselines across multiple hardware setups. The result supports treating speculative decoding as a joint algorithm-and-runtime problem. In this approach, the usefulness of a draft depends on its execution cost as well as its role in generating tokens, and the tree structure helps accommodate both.
neurips-2025-yggdrasil-bridging-dynamic-.tldr: Yggdrasil coordinates tree-based speculative drafting with static runtime execution, reporting up to 3.98-fold speedups without modifying the language model.

paragraphs: Clustering tables is difficult because the meaning of similarity changes between datasets. Without labels, choosing hyperparameters for deep clustering methods is also challenging and can lead to unstable results. ZEUS aims to reduce this dependence on dataset-specific choices by applying a pretrained model directly to previously unseen tabular data.

The model learns from synthetic datasets generated using a latent-variable prior. At application time, it decomposes a complex dataset into meaningful components and produces representations that can be clustered effectively. It requires no additional training or fine-tuning on the new dataset. This places the learning effort in pretraining and makes the resulting clustering capability available without per-dataset intervention.

Experiments show performance matching or exceeding traditional clustering algorithms and recent deep-learning methods, alongside substantially greater speed and ease of use. The authors describe ZEUS as, to their knowledge, the first fully unsupervised zero-shot embedding method for tabular data. Its main contribution is demonstrating that synthetic pretraining can support useful clustering representations across varied datasets without repeatedly fitting a new representation model.
neurips-2025-zeus-zero-shot-embeddings-f.tldr: ZEUS learns from synthetic tables to produce clustering representations for new datasets without additional training or fine-tuning.
